$comment: Implementation status for the Tool Mode specifications. Consumed by scripts/gen-traceability.mjs. Anything absent here is reported as NOT_RUN. Update this file as work lands; never edit TRACEABILITY.md by hand.

notes.MCP-01: VERIFIED BLOCKER: the latest published @modelcontextprotocol/sdk (1.32.1) declares LATEST_PROTOCOL_VERSION=2025-11-25 and SUPPORTED_PROTOCOL_VERSIONS=[2025-11-25,2025-06-18,2025-03-26,2024-11-05,2024-10-07]. It does NOT support 2026-07-28. That revision IS published upstream (schema/2026-07-28/ and a 2026-07-28 git tag exist in modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol), so MCP-01's 'separately reviewed, schema-conformant adaptation' clause is the route that must be taken: the wire layer has to be implemented against the official schema rather than delegated to the SDK.
notes.DEC-01: VERIFIED BLOCKER: the npm package `laya-ts` named by DEC-02 does not exist (registry returns 404). No published Node entry point for Laya was found on npm. Milestone D's Laya default cannot be qualified until a real distribution channel is identified; BASE-14 forbids substituting an unrelated model silently.
notes.DEC-02: BLOCKED on the same missing `laya-ts` package. DEC-02 additionally requires a maintainer-run ONNX export in controlled CI plus numerical-parity evidence, which cannot be executed here without the source checkpoint and Python toolchain.
notes.NDL-01: PARTIAL EVIDENCE: cactus-compute/needle exists on GitHub (13,894 stars; 'automation foundation model for tiny devices') and as a Hugging Face repo. No node-named npm distribution for Needle 3 was found (@cactus-compute/needle and needle-ai both 404; `cactus-needle@0.3.0` exists but is unverified against NDL-01's requirements). The NDL-01 runtime strategy is therefore unqualified.
notes.MODEL-01: PARTIAL EVIDENCE: google/embeddinggemma-2 exists on Hugging Face (124,930 downloads, ungated); google/embeddinggemma-300m exists but is gated=manual, which would require the operator to accept terms before download. sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 are both present and ungated, matching BASE-12's preserved 384-dimensional space.
notes.AT-01: NOT_RUN: requires a clean compatible DSH installation and a built tarball install. The current package is published and installable (verified for @try-works/dsh-model-as-tool@0.1.1), but the Tool Mode bundle does not exist yet.
notes.AT-04: NOT_RUN and currently unreachable: requires a genuine 2026-07-28 reference client. The published SDK cannot speak that revision, so the client side must come from the schema-conformant adaptation described under MCP-01.

BASE-01.evidence: Catalog, adapters, skills, persistence and platform checks preserved; the plugin was extended in place across commits fcb79ea..2e27e2a rather than recreated.

BASE-02.evidence: Tool identity is now independent of model identity: a catalog `contract` binding decides the tool name, the host registers ONE tool per contract, and a two-implementation catalog test proves two models yield one `lang_detect`. Adapter factories are now keyed on the npm PACKAGE rather than the model id, because keying on the id was itself a model-name switch that made a second conforming implementation unservable. Provider override is host config with documented fallback. Remaining: the merge is proven with test fixtures, not with two distinct real models.

BASE-03.evidence: `stt_transcribe` is now the canonical registered name and `transcribe_audio` is an opt-in alias (`legacyAliases`, default false) so it stays out of the default catalog. Tests assert the alias is absent by default, appears only when enabled, and keeps its own argument shape (`audio_path`) rather than being reinterpreted as the canonical contract's (`audio.path`). Remaining: not exercised against a real recording.

BASE-04.evidence: Explicit requiredness comes from the contract schema required array; parameter-order inference is gone from the contract path. Real per-tool output schemas are enforced by Ajv on every result. DSH cannot advertise every JSON-Schema keyword, so the projection reports what it omits and argument validation enforces it against the untouched contract (tested: minLength is reported as runtime-enforced and still rejects a short value). Remaining: the legacy per-model registrar path still infers requiredness from parameter order.

MODEL-01.evidence: Availability verified only: google/embeddinggemma-2 exists on Hugging Face ungated (124,930 downloads). No adapter, packaging or modality test exists yet.

DECL-01.evidence: Contracts are authored once with stable name, identity, version, input/output schema, semantics, limits and unsupported cases; DSH parameter projection is generated from that one source. MCP projection and Code Mode type generation are not implemented.

DECL-02.evidence: The EXT-32 addition was REFUSED at runtime by the control tool output schema before it was declared, which is the schema discipline working: undeclared fields are rejected rather than passed through. The new provenance, readiness, callable and withheld fields are now declared explicitly with additionalProperties false at every level, so the discovery shape cannot drift unnoticed. Remaining: the DSH tool declarations themselves are still built by the registrar rather than generated from the publication surface.

DECL-03.evidence: ToolMeta is defined once and now STAMPED BY THE HOST on every contract-registered call: extension/version/receipt come from host state and the implementation cannot forge them. Tests assert the envelope, the implementation id that actually ran, distinct receipts per call, and that an adapter cannot override the host identity. Remaining: host stamping covers contract-registered tools only.

DECL-04.evidence: Contracts declare scoreKind/calibrated, and a fabricated `confidence` field is refused by output validation (tested). Not yet enforced across the whole tool surface.

TOOL-01.evidence: The stt.transcribe contract declares transcription-not-translation, seconds from start-of-audio, empty-is-valid, partial coverage via coverage.complete, error-on-unsupported-timestamp, and the admitted 16 kHz mono PCM16 WAV limits. No implementation is bound and no real audio has been transcribed through it.

TOOL-03.evidence: The text.language_detect contract preserves ambiguity (candidates + tooCloseToCall), declares scoreKind, and states that it is written-text-only and not evidence about spoken audio. Not yet bound to an implementation through the contract.

DEC-01.evidence: No distribution channel: npm `laya-ts` returns 404 and no published Node entry point for Laya was found. Needs an operator decision (see note).

DEC-02.evidence: Same missing `laya-ts` entry point, plus DEC-02 requires a maintainer-run ONNX export in CI with numerical-parity evidence, which needs the source checkpoint and a Python toolchain.

NDL-01.evidence: Needle exists upstream (github.com/cactus-compute/needle, HF cactus-compute/needle) but no verified Node/WASM distribution for Needle 3 was found; the runtime strategy is unqualified.

BASE-05.evidence: The host now constructs an InvocationAuthority from an operator-built grant and passes it to every adapter, so a request cannot supply or widen it. It carries grantId, caller kind, limits, recording policy and a resolvePath bound to the approved roots; a test asserts the object exposes no mutable roots list. SEC-03 tool grants and SEC-10 destination grants are enforced before inference. Remaining: filesystem access is wired into the Voz path tool but not every adapter, and the harness-executor/capability fields of SEC-03 do not exist yet.

SEC-03.evidence: createGrant models allowedTools, approvedRoots, remoteDestinations, hostedCode, recordingPolicy and limits; authorizeTool/authorizeDestination refuse before any model work. Defaults are conservative (no hosted code, no recording, no roots, so it fails closed). Remaining: per-application independently revocable credentials (SEC-01) and harness-executor profiles are not implemented, and the interactive grant covers the standard tools rather than being created per client.

SEC-06.evidence: authorizePath resolves drive letters, separators, Unicode, junctions and symlinks via realpathSync.native, then checks containment on a separator boundary; it refuses relative paths, UNC and Windows device paths, NUL bytes, missing paths and anything outside every root, and returns the CANONICAL path so the caller opens what was authorized rather than re-resolving it (closing the check-then-open race). Tested against real directories and real Windows junctions, including Unicode and space-containing valid paths, a sibling whose name shares a prefix, traversal, and links that stay inside. 1 of 24 cases skipped where the platform forbids file symlinks without elevation; the equivalent junction case covers that escape.

SEC-10.evidence: authorizeDestination refuses an unauthorized remote destination, and the grant exposes no silent local-to-remote fallback path. Remaining: the hosted-code and harness-executor edges of the rule are not implemented.

EXT-13.evidence: discoverExtension reads package.json and the manifest as BOUNDED data (256 KB / 512 KB limits) and never imports the entry: the test fixture writes an entry that throws on import, and reaching the assertions proves it never ran. It enforces name, version, type:module, an explicit exports map, the toolMode.manifest field, containment of the manifest path, and rejects malformed or oversized JSON as INVALID_EXTENSION. Remaining: quarantine fetch, archive inspection and the install/activate lifecycle are not implemented.

EXT-14.evidence: extension-manifest-1.1.0.schema.json ships with the SDK and is enforced at runtime via Ajv 2020-12. Beyond the schema it checks exact id/version agreement with the package, unique local ids per contribution kind, duplicate caller-facing tool NAMES reported as TOOL_NAME_CONFLICT, referenced files that must exist, paths that must not escape the package, and unknown REQUIRED features blocking activation as INCOMPATIBLE_PROTOCOL. Unknown top-level fields are rejected while the x- vendor namespace is admitted. Remaining: asset-lock validation (EXT-15) and keyed digests.

EXT-16.evidence: A 1.0 manifest is normalized to module execution as a VIEW, leaving the input object untouched so the recorded digest still describes the installed bytes; the lift provenance is attached after validation rather than smuggled past the closed schema. Protocol 1.1.0, runtime API major 1, and the five separate identities are documented in code. Remaining: minor-version conformance tests and the contract/recipe/model revision separation are not implemented end to end.

EXT-17.evidence: The SDK now defines and exports the complete public runtime API: ToolModeExtensionV1, ExtensionContextV1, ExtensionInstanceV1, ModelProviderV1, ProviderInspectionV1, PreparedAssetMapV1, InvocationContextV1, JsonObject/JsonValue, the DisposeReason vocabulary, defineExtension() which rejects a wrong apiVersion at the declaration site, and the reserved-meta guard. Loading is implemented in load.ts: the entry is resolved from the package own exports map rather than a convention, the shape is validated BEFORE create() runs, and a missing dispose() is refused because a host with no way to release an instance could never fully stop it. Remaining: the declarative interpreter, the conformance helpers, and the reference test host with a fake harness broker are not implemented, and the SDK is not published to npm.

EXT-25.evidence: The six dimensions are modelled separately and now PERSIST: a profile state file round-trips installation, desired and observed activation, per-deployment readiness, per-profile tool selection with the selected implementation, and export authorization independently, with profiles kept apart. A corrupt or oversized file, or one malformed entry, invalidates the whole file rather than dropping just the bad part, because a file that is demonstrably untrustworthy must not activate anything. Remaining: activation does not yet write these states, so persistence is exercised by tests rather than by a lifecycle operation.

EXT-34.evidence: All 15 published codes exist with the operation, safe recovery advice and a retryable flag DERIVED from the code so a permission refusal cannot be mistaken for a transient fault. Recovery text is passed through a sanitiser that strips credential- and path-shaped spans. Remaining: the codes are not yet raised by install/activate/uninstall, which do not exist.

EXT-07.evidence: stagedInstall returns `activation: "inactive"` as an explicit field so a caller cannot mistake a successful install for a usable tool, and it imports nothing: the test fixture ships an entry that THROWS on import, so reaching the assertions proves installation never executed it. No inference, no warming, no tool or skill publication. Remaining: no inventory and no activation path, so the state an install produces is not yet persisted or readable.

EXT-08.evidence: The ordered pipeline runs and now RECORDS its result: fetch into a unique quarantine directory -> verify SHA-512 -> list entries -> validate the entry list -> extract -> discover as data -> promote by atomic rename -> record in the store lock -> remove quarantine on every path. Recording happens AFTER the bytes are in place, because a lock entry naming a directory that does not exist would make verification report a missing installation as a changed one. Remaining: dependency resolution and locking, the permission/licence/platform preview, and operator approval are not implemented.

EXT-11.evidence: Entry-list validation refuses traversal, absolute paths, drive letters, UNC, backslashes, NUL bytes, Windows reserved device names, segments ending in a dot or space, duplicates, Windows case collisions, symlinks and hardlinks, plus entry-count, per-entry, total-byte and expansion-ratio bounds. Tested against REAL zip archives built at the byte level, because adm-zip sanitizes entry names on write and therefore cannot produce the hostile archives these defenses exist to refuse; a raw ZIP writer in the test suite supplies the bytes. The extractor re-asserts confinement at the write, so a bypassed validator still cannot escape. Remaining: fetch time limits are passed through but not enforced by the SDK, which owns no network stack.

EXT-33.evidence: The store now RECORDS what it installs: an operator-owned extensions.lock.json holds complete resolved source/identity records (identity, version, install path, archive digest, CONTENT digest, source, timestamp), so identity survives restart and a package edited on disk after installation is detected before activation rather than trusted. Version-keyed layout keeps two versions side by side. Corrupted state FAILS CLOSED: a lock or profile file that cannot be trusted yields NO records and a diagnostic, never a fallback to "everything installed is active", and a lock that could not be read is refused as an append target rather than silently overwritten. All writes are atomic (temp plus rename) and a failed write throws instead of reporting success. Remaining: per-install dependency locks and transaction records are not implemented, and cleanup-pending tombstones do not exist.

EXT-26.evidence: Activation verifies the installed bytes and locks BEFORE publishing anything (a package edited after installation is refused as INTEGRITY_MISMATCH with nothing published), persists intended-active before publication so a crash leaves a record rather than a silent no-op, publishes every required contribution through an injected registrar, and commits the catalog generation ONLY once all of them were accepted. A failed registration rolls back narrowly: only the handles this activation published are withdrawn, the generation does not advance, and a healthy extension stays active AND callable - tested with one good and one failing package in the same profile. Readiness is assessed rather than assumed: merely unprepared assets activate with needs-preparation diagnostics as EXT-26 requires, while a FAILED deployment refuses activation because it will not become ready by waiting. Remaining: no managed worker is started and the public entry/API is not validated, because there is no worker runtime; provider handles are not created.

EXT-27.evidence: Deactivation persists inactive intent before withdrawing, withdraws contributions, and refuses to claim a full stop when it cannot confirm one. A NEW CASE was found while writing the CLI tests: a fresh process (or a CLI not attached to the host) holds no publication handles, so it cannot withdraw another process's contributions. It previously reported a clean stop in that situation, which is the exact lie EXT-27 forbids. The lifecycle now detects an extension recorded as active while this instance holds no handles and reports the cleanup failure with guidance to stop the owning host, leaving the state quarantined. Remaining: active calls are not cancelled, disposal hooks are not called, no grace period is joined, and no owned process is terminated, because there is no worker runtime.

EXT-28.evidence: Uninstalling an active package returns EXTENSION_IN_USE unless deactivation is explicitly requested, and the CLI now prints the impact preview (affected profile and each contributed tool) before refusing, as EXT-28 requires. With --deactivate the deactivation sequence runs first, the record is removed, the disabled tombstone is RETAINED so nothing silently resurrects the package, and --purge-assets reports that deletion may complete after restart on Windows. Remaining: private resolved dependencies are not deleted, credential references and executable-content approvals are not revoked, and BUILTIN_PROTECTED is not reachable because nothing is marked built-in.

EXT-04.evidence: Every extension is deactivatable through the same path, a built-in being a first-party package rather than an exception. Individual tools toggle independently of activation: disabling one tool leaves the package active and its other tools callable, and toggling an unknown tool is refused rather than ignored. Uninstall is implemented for third-party packages with the EXTENSION_IN_USE gate. Remaining: BUILTIN_PROTECTED is unreachable because nothing is marked built-in yet, and asset purging does not exist.

BASE-09.evidence: The host holds no model-specific code, and the property is now ENFORCED rather than inspected. `npm run verify:architecture` fails the build on three shapes of a private built-in path: a vendor SDK import, a branch on a literal model id, and a non-empty ADAPTER_FACTORIES. The rules match SHAPE rather than a list of known model names, because a rule enumerating today's models would pass the day a new one is added, which is exactly when it must fail. PROVEN TO FIRE: the gate was run against the real code this repository shipped before the extraction (the `entry.id === 'tongue'` branch in registrar.ts, the two-entry ADAPTER_FACTORIES list, the vendor import) and rejects all three, and re-introducing the registrar branch into the working tree fails the gate with the offending file and line. It distinguishes configuration from a built-in: comparing against an operator-configured provider override is accepted, the same shape written with a literal is rejected, and comments documenting a prohibition do not satisfy it. Both extraction requirements are satisfied: model implementations live in independently versioned packages reached only through the public extension API, and both packages are built and linked.

EXT-02.evidence: The prohibition is now mechanically checked rather than conventional: the architecture gate rejects an extension that imports the host package by path, imports DSH, or climbs out of its own package with a relative import, and it runs over both shipped extensions as part of `npm run verify`. Both extensions import only @try-works/tool-mode-extension-sdk, with the vendor model packages reached through a dynamic import at load time rather than a static dependency. Remaining: the check covers the packages in this repository and would not see a third-party extension published elsewhere; enforcing it for those needs a packaging-time check on the consumer side.

EXT-18.evidence: All five named context contracts exist with the required semantics documented: ExtensionContextV1 carries host-issued identity, private storage, a bounded logger and a teardown signal, and deliberately NO DSH ctx, registry mutation, global credentials or unfiltered environment; ProviderInspectionV1 reports readiness/features/missing/runtimeVersion and inspection is implemented to read only approved local state (a test asserts it reports unprepared before a load rather than claiming ready); PreparedAssetMapV1 and InvocationContextV1 carry verified handles and call-scoped grants with no caller-supplied authority. Remaining: the asset map is a type without a host implementation, and the file/network broker operations are typed but have no enforcing host behind them.

EXT-19.evidence: Import and create() are lightweight and tested: the extension declares no assets because Tongue bundles its weights, module import performs no work, and a test asserts createProvider returns a handle in well under a second rather than parsing the weight file, with inspect() reporting unprepared until load() is called. Disposal is idempotent and the host disposes providers per model and instances per extension. Remaining: there is no pooling, no concurrency admission, and unload() is only a cache drop because no provider holds a process-level resource yet.

EXT-31.evidence: The full required command family exists and runs as `dsh-tool-mode`: extensions list|inspect|install|activate|prepare|deactivate|uninstall and tools enable|disable, with --store, --profile and --integrity. The logic is a library entry taking argv and an output sink, so the REFUSAL paths are tested as directly as the happy ones rather than being left to manual checking. INSTALL REQUIRES --integrity: an install with no verifiable digest is refused, because EXT-12 makes integrity the record that later verification depends on and an unverified install cannot be undone. OFFLINE EDITS TAKE EXCLUSIVE STORE OWNERSHIP: mutating commands acquire store.lock, refuse when a live process holds it, treat a dead holder as stale rather than blocking forever, and release only their own lock. Uninstall of an active extension refuses and shows the impact preview (profiles and tools) before naming --deactivate. Deactivation that cannot confirm a full stop reports a quarantine rather than a clean result. Remaining: there is no running-host management channel, so commands act offline only; the management surface is deliberately absent from the inference tool surface as EXT-31 requires, but the settings actions and the MCP-side management grant do not exist.

EXT-24.evidence: Publication is built WHOLE and consulted before anything is registered. buildSurface produces a complete surface from the candidates, the host registers a tool only when that surface actually published it, and an incoherent surface is refused rather than partially applied. The rules EXT-24 states absolutely are enforced and tested: a tool without a runnable implementation binding is withheld (no-implementation) because a schema alone is a promise nothing can keep; a FAILED deployment is withheld with the reason that waiting will not help; an UNPREPARED model publishes readiness and a preparation skill but NOT a working inference tool; a USAGE skill is withheld unless every tool it requires is visible, naming the missing tool; duplicate tool names are REFUSED rather than silently resolved, because a name identifies one tool; and every withholding is reported with a code, subject and owner rather than dropped silently. The surface carries a generation and swaps as a whole through one callback receiving both sides, so a consumer never infers the change from a partially-updated view. Skill provenance is tracked: orphanedSkills names the skills whose owning extension is gone. Remaining: DSH tool declarations, MCP discovery and Code Mode type discovery are not yet updated from the generation - only the host tool registration consults it - and readiness is currently always "ready" for a runnable model because no preparation lifecycle exists, so the needs-preparation path is proven by test rather than by a real deployment.

EXT-32.evidence: Discovery now exposes public extension/implementation provenance and readiness per model, through the real tool pipeline: contract, extension package, modelId inside that package, the tool name actually published, and the alternatives not selected, plus a readiness value and a callable flag. An ABSENT tool is explicable rather than merely missing - a model that cannot run on this host reports callable false, and a withheld contribution reports its surface code and message. The shape is TOTAL: every row carries every field, including for a model with no contract or extension binding, so a caller never handles a partially-populated model. One helper computes the publication decision for both the installer and discovery, because two call sites computing it separately is how a tool gets registered while discovery reports it withheld. The listing discloses no filesystem layout or approved roots. Remaining: tool_mode_list and tool_mode_describe themselves are not created - this extends the existing model_tools surface - external callers are not yet filtered to authorized information, the model_tools migration is not documented, and no management grant exists for installer/update/uninstall bindings.

EXT-35.evidence: Invocation receipts and lifecycle records exist as SEPARATE structures, because mixing them would let a caller reading a receipt learn about operator actions it has no business seeing and would make an audit trail indistinguishable from execution metadata. A receipt records the extension package, its version, the content digest, the dependency-lock digest, the model/recipe identity, the activation generation and the execution location; the content digest is what lets two runs of the SAME version be told apart, since a package can be replaced at one version. Receipts are emitted on every SUCCESSFUL call and NOT on a refused one, because a receipt for a call that failed validation would claim provenance for a result nobody received; verified through the real pipeline, including that the invoked text never appears in a receipt. The metadata-only rule is enforced by CONSTRUCTION: buildInvocationReceipt takes only host-resolved inputs, so there is no parameter through which a body, token or skill text could arrive, and every warning passes a redactor that strips npm/GitHub/bearer tokens and absolute paths of either shape. redactPath reduces a path to its leaf plus a short digest, so an operator can correlate two receipts without learning the filesystem layout. Lifecycle records carry the operation, outcome, profile and approving principal, refuse an operator approval with no identity, and carry no execution fields. The log policy defaults to quiet, metadata-only, telemetry off, and REFUSES an undeclared network origin rather than logging it. Remaining: receipts are retained in a bounded in-memory ring, not persisted to a receipt store; lifecycle records are built but not yet emitted by the CLI or the lifecycle; the store still records no dependency-lock digest, so that field is always null; and extension logging is not yet driven through the policy by a real extension.

MCP-01.evidence: A schema-conformant adaptation of revision 2026-07-28 exists, and conformance is now VERIFIED AGAINST THE PINNED UPSTREAM SCHEMA rather than against a reading of the prose. The official schema.json, schema.ts and schema.mdx are pinned under docs/tool-mode/specs/mcp-2026-07-28/ at commit 5f5440bb26a62e2cf3440b92da5a667efa03b267 (resolved from the 2026-07-28 tag, so the pin is immutable rather than a moving ref), with SHA-256 digests asserted by test so a later edit to the pinned copy is detected. It is a self-contained 2020-12 schema with no remote $ref, checked by test. Pinning immediately found THREE REAL CONFORMANCE ERRORS in code that had passed every hand-written test: a DiscoverResult carrying three fields the definition does not declare and NONE of the five it requires; a ListToolsResult missing cacheScope and ttlMs, which the definition requires; and a metadata parser requiring clientInfo where the schema makes it optional, so it rejected requests the schema admits. All three are fixed and every message the server sends is now validated against the pinned definitions by Ajv (DiscoverResultResponse, ListToolsResultResponse, CallToolResultResponse for both success and tool-error, JSONRPCErrorResponse, HeaderMismatchError). Remaining: the HTTP transport, SSE response channel, subscriptions/listen, normalised cancellation and the stdio bridge executable do not exist; the protocol/client compatibility matrix is not yet recorded as a released artifact.

MCP-04.evidence: A modern tools/list and tools/call are proven to be processable as the FIRST application request with no initialize handshake and no session, because the dispatch layer is stateless by construction. Evidence is now an artifact rather than an assertion: the fixture corpus captures both as first requests, and the independently-authored probe validates them against the pinned upstream schema. The COMPATIBILITY MATRIX is recorded in docs/tool-mode/fixtures/mcp-2026-07-28/MANIFEST.json: the exact revision, the pinned schema commit, the official SDK version, and the fact that the SDK does NOT support this revision, so this server is the schema-conformant adaptation MCP-01 permits rather than an SDK configuration. Remaining: the SDK version currently reads not-installed because the official SDK is not a dependency of this repository, so the matrix records its absence rather than a version. No legacy translation mode is offered or tested. A report asserting only a 2026-07-28 string equality would still fail the gate, which is why the probe asserts schema conformance of actual message bodies per fixture instead.

MCP-05.evidence: server/discover returns the revision, the server identity and the full feature matrix including what is NOT implemented, so a client can distinguish absent from unmentioned. Tool discovery and invocation are implemented with deterministic ordering and a JSON-RPC error for an unknown method rather than a pretence of service. Remaining: authorized catalog subscriptions (subscriptions/listen), transport-specific cancellation, and the HTTP endpoint itself are not implemented.

MCP-06.evidence: tools/list is deterministically ordered (asserted), and the surface lists what the host reports as authorized rather than a global catalog. The publication surface already withholds a tool whose selected implementation is not callable and reports readiness instead (EXT-24), so an unprepared catalog entry does not become an inference leaf. Remaining: the caller-permitted set is not yet computed per grant at the MCP boundary, and the requirement that installed-but-cold models count as callable is not exercised because there is no preparation lifecycle.

MCP-09.evidence: The canonical OUTPUT schema is exported, and the provenance is asserted rather than assumed: derivePayloadSchema removes ONLY the reserved root meta property and its required entry, per the section 16.4 derivation, and tests prove every other property and constraint survives verbatim and that the derivation does not mutate the shared contract. Both schemas come from the CONTRACTS, never from DSH model-facing schemas() projection, which intentionally omits output. The fact is observable through the control tool: a new read-only mcp action reports each exported tool and whether it has an output schema, with a test asserting every one does, and another asserting the exported set EQUALS the registered set, so MCP cannot advertise something the host withheld. Remaining: the schemas are exported but no client has been driven against them end to end, and a tool that is registered but whose model is unprepared still appears, because the publication surface treats a runnable model as ready in the absence of a preparation lifecycle.

MCP-10.evidence: The finalized canonical value is returned in structuredContent with a bounded model-readable content rendering, and the two error kinds are kept distinct in both directions, each with a test: an application failure is a SUCCESSFUL protocol response carrying isError with resultType complete, while an infrastructure failure, an unknown tool and malformed arguments are JSON-RPC errors with no result member. An unknown tool is deliberately invalid params rather than a tool error, because nothing was invoked and a domain failure would be a fabrication. Remaining: the bounded content rendering is a plain text projection rather than a content-block policy, and the post-policy canonical value is whatever the host returns, since no result policy layer exists yet.

MCP-13.evidence: A tool whose definition reports importedFromMcp is refused at dispatch with invalid params and never invoked, asserted by a test that also checks the host was not called, because re-exporting would let a server delegate back into itself through a loop no caller can see. Remaining: nothing yet produces an imported MCP tool, so the guard is exercised against a stub rather than against a real import path.

MCP-14.evidence: The revision declared TTL/cache-scope mechanism is used: cacheable results carry cacheScope private and ttlMs 0, which the pinned CacheableResult definition REQUIRES on DiscoverResult and ListToolsResult alike, asserted by test and by schema validation. Zero TTL with a private scope is the correct default for an authorization-filtered catalog: a shared cache keyed on tool names would leak one caller permitted set to another. Remaining: nothing caches yet, so the fields state the policy rather than govern a cache; authorization is not recomputed per invocation at the MCP boundary because the caller-permitted set is not yet computed there.

MCP-02.evidence: The loopback HTTP endpoint exists and is proven to bind and serve a real request over a real socket: startHttpServer refuses a non-loopback bind address AT STARTUP rather than warning and binding anyway, which is the only enforcement that cannot be forgotten later, and it listens on the loopback interface specifically rather than on all interfaces. The path, port and body limit are configurable, defaulting to /mcp, 3765 and 4 MiB. The handler is a pure function of a request description, so every refusal path is testable without a port. Remaining: no TLS (loopback only, so none is needed), and LAN/public binding is out of scope for the first release as the requirement states.

MCP-03.evidence: The stdio bridge exists as a library (src/mcp/stdio.ts) and an executable (bin/dsh-tool-mode-mcp-stdio.mjs), and per P26-05 it is an HTTP CLIENT rather than a second protocol implementation: it generates the modern per-request headers and posts to the same endpoint a network client uses, so there is no second interpretation of the protocol to drift out of step. Two simultaneous authorized clients with independently revocable credentials are proven against one host surface, and a client credential is refused by another client endpoint. Remain: the stdout-purity property of the executable is verified STATICALLY rather than by running it, because this sandbox cannot spawn a child with piped stdio (named pipes are blocked); the check asserts there are exactly two stdout writes and that both are protocol frames, that every diagnostic goes through a named stderr sink, and that console.log does not appear at all. That is weaker than an end-to-end run and is recorded as such.

SEC-02.evidence: All five named controls are implemented and tested: the LOOPBACK check reads the socket address rather than a caller-supplied header, because trusting a header would make the binding decorative; Host is therefore not the check; approved ORIGINS are an allow-list and an unapproved browser origin is refused while a request with no Origin is admitted, which is the non-browser case; request SIZE is limited and the limit is enforced DURING the read rather than after it, since buffering an unbounded body to measure it defeats the limit; and AUTHENTICATION is required on every request including discovery, with the token compared in constant time and never echoed in a failure response. CORS is not authentication, proven by a test where an approved origin with a bad token still returns 401. Remaining: the OAuth 2.1 resource-server profile is not implemented, so audience and scope validation do not exist.

P26-15.evidence: Static-token custom authentication is implemented and is explicitly NOT claimed as OAuth: authProfile() reports oauth21ResourceServer false with a note stating the profile is not implemented and is not claimed, and claimsOAuthConformance() returns false so a status report or compatibility matrix cannot assert otherwise by accident. Plain unauthenticated loopback is not available: every request including server/discover needs a credential. Credentials are per-client and independently revocable in the sense that each client endpoint validates its own token. Remaining: no OAuth 2.1 resource-server implementation, no protected-resource or authorization-server metadata, no audience or scope validation, no challenge flow beyond a bare WWW-Authenticate: Bearer, and no dynamic registration. P26-15 permits the static-token mode only while forbidding the conformance claim, which is the line this implementation holds.

P26-16.evidence: Tested here: origin rejection, invalid and missing tokens, mixed clients with independent credentials, token leakage (a failure response is asserted not to contain either the configured token or the presented one), and header/version errors. Remaining: expired and wrong-audience tokens and insufficient scopes do not exist because there is no OAuth profile; bridge credential protection is untested because the bridge does not exist; headless operation fails with actionable guidance for a missing token but no interactive approval path exists.

P26-07.evidence: No resumability is implemented, and the absence is asserted rather than assumed: sending Last-Event-ID changes neither the status nor the body, because there is no replay path to enter, and the response advertises no event-stream channel it does not serve. A retry is therefore a new request with fresh authorization, which is what the requirement asks for. This is a small requirement satisfied by not building the thing it forbids.

P26-08.evidence: The requirements are implemented and each has a test: stdout carries protocol traffic and NOTHING else while diagnostics go through a separate named sink, so there is no single output to confuse; the request body is forwarded VERBATIM so ids and per-request metadata cannot drift between the two hops, with the bridge regenerating only the headers; nothing is retained between requests except in-flight cancellation state keyed by request id and removed when the request settles, so one stdio process is not treated as one conversation; EOF aborts bridge-owned in-flight requests and sends nothing to the host, which is shared and not the bridge to stop; and a malformed frame is answered on the PROTOCOL channel because a client waiting for a reply would not see a diagnostic. Remaining: the executable is not run end-to-end (sandbox limitation above), and a legacy stdio translation mode is neither offered nor tested.

P26-06.evidence: Stdio cancellation uses notifications/cancelled and aborts EXACTLY the referenced request: a test holds two requests in flight, cancels one, and asserts the first signal is aborted while the second is NOT, which is the property that stops one cancellation tearing down a shared worker. A cancellation for a request the bridge does not own is reported rather than ignored, because that usually means the client and bridge disagree about what is in flight. A JSON response channel is implemented. Remaining: no request-scoped SSE response channel, so closing an HTTP SSE response cannot cancel its request; cancellation is not translated into an HTTP abort of a request sharing a bridge or model worker in the network direction, because there is no SSE stream to close.

MCP-08.evidence: The MCP surface is now bound to the real registry: a new mcp/host-binding.ts builds the surface over the contracts the activation actually REGISTERED, so it cannot advertise a tool the publication surface withheld, and invocation is routed through the DSH tool runtime ctx.tools.execute(). A test asserts the SERVER-ISSUED call identity reaches the executor and that a distinct one is issued per invocation, because a caller-supplied identity would let a caller forge a receipt, and it asserts the executor receives the CALLER OWN signal so cancellation reaches the actual work. A host failure is reported as a tool error rather than a fabricated success. Remaining: no test drives a full tools/call through dispatch into a real inference call, because the models this host can run are not prepared; the caller-permitted set is not computed per grant at the MCP boundary; and native input validation is the contract validation already applied by the registered tool body rather than a separate MCP-side check.

MCP-12.evidence: A tool that cannot be exported faithfully is withheld ENTIRELY with a recorded reason rather than partly serialized, and onWithheld reports it so the reason is not lost. Writing the tests found a real bug in this: callTool looked for the tool in the published set, which INCLUDES withheld tools, so a client that guessed the name could invoke exactly the tool the export deliberately refused to promise - defeating the requirement through the back door. It now checks exportability as well as presence, and a test covers it. Remaining: nothing yet produces a notExportableReason, so the path is exercised against a fixture rather than by a real non-exportable host tool; TMX extension tools are not yet routed through this same mapping.

MCP-17.evidence: A fixture corpus and a SEPARATELY AUTHORED PROBE exist. Fifteen sanitized fixtures are captured as FROZEN FILES under docs/tool-mode/fixtures/mcp-2026-07-28/, covering discovery, tool invocation (success and domain failure), header and version errors, missing metadata, an unknown tool, an unknown method, unauthenticated access, a non-loopback peer, concurrency and cancellation. Each records what it demonstrates and the expectation an auditor can check. The probe (scripts/probe-mcp-conformance.mjs) is independent by construction: it reads the frozen files from disk, imports none of the server, dispatch or protocol modules, and validates against the PINNED upstream schema with Ajv, so it cannot inherit a mistake from the code that produced the fixtures. It runs in npm run verify and reports 34 checks with 0 failures. The manifest pins the schema by immutable commit and records the official SDK version together with the note that the SDK cannot speak this revision, which is part of the MCP-04 answer. The probe found FOUR real defects on first run: two fixtures that LIED about what they demonstrated (a loopback-refusal case captured from the loopback address, and a domain-failure case that used an unpublished tool name so it recorded an invalid-params error instead), a JSON-RPC error carrying id null which the pinned RequestId type does not admit, and a mapping bug in the probe itself. What it does NOT establish is stated in the probe header: the fixtures were produced by this repository own code, so the probe shows the CAPTURED BYTES satisfy the upstream definitions, not that every possible request would. Remaining: subscription and SSE fixtures are absent because those surfaces do not exist, and the selected-SDK half of the requirement cannot be met while the official SDK cannot speak 2026-07-28 - this is an adaptation, so there is no independent SDK side to cross-check against.

AT-13.evidence: Windows traversal, absolute-path escape, junction escape, device/UNC paths and unauthorized roots are all refused, with Unicode and space-containing valid paths admitted (authority.test.ts, real filesystem). Remaining: the artifact/receipt identifier half of the test, which needs a receipt store that does not exist yet.

AT-01.evidence: Requires a clean compatible DSH installation and a built tarball of the Tool Mode bundle. The packages build and install individually, but the bundle does not exist yet.

AT-18.evidence: The durable-write half is satisfied for the extension store: a write that fails throws rather than reporting success, all writes go through a temporary file and a rename, and no temporary file survives. Corrupted state fails closed with a diagnostic rather than enabling every installed package. Remaining: the migration half (existing enable/disable choices surviving an upgrade) is not exercised, because the extension store has no prior format to migrate from.
